title: Women’s political representation is edging forward while executive power, parliamentary leadership, and safety remain sharply unequal
source_unit: Inter-Parliamentary Union and UN Women, Women in Politics: 2026 and Women in Parliament 2025 reporting
geography: Global national parliaments, cabinets, heads of state or government, parliamentary speakers, women parliamentarians, and countries holding elections or parliamentary renewals in 2025

denominator.unit: countries and national political institutions covered by IPU-UN Women Women in Politics 2026 data

women_parliamentary_seats.unit: percent of national parliamentary seats held by women worldwide

women_cabinet_posts.unit: percent of cabinet minister positions held by women worldwide

women_heads_state_or_government.unit: countries led by a woman Head of State or Government in 2026

countries_never_woman_leader.unit: countries that have never had a woman leader

cabinet_parity_countries.unit: countries that have achieved gender parity in cabinet

observations.method: IPU and UN Women compilation of official political leadership, cabinet, and parliamentary representation data as of 1 January 2026.
observations.uncertainty: Representation counts describe formal officeholding, not policy influence, constituency service, agenda control, political preferences, or outcomes for women and other groups.
observations.subgroup: Women and men in national political institutions, candidates, parties, voters, cabinets, parliaments, and countries with different electoral systems and quotas.
observations.counterinterpretation: Descriptive representation can coexist with limited authority, while small numerical gains can still change norms, networks, and policy attention; parity in one institution does not establish equal power across the system.

denominator.unit: national parliamentary seats and Speakers of Parliament worldwide

parliamentary_change.unit: percentage-point increase in women's share of parliamentary seats from 2025 to 2026

women_speakers.unit: percent of Speakers of Parliament who were women as of January 2026

women_speakers_count.unit: women serving as Speakers of Parliament as of January 2026

new_speaker_share.unit: percent of 75 new Speakers appointed or elected in 2025 who were women

progress_pattern.value: parliamentary representation gained slowly while women’s share of parliamentary speakers declined

observations.method: IPU annual comparison of parliamentary composition, parliamentary leadership, and countries holding parliamentary renewals in 2025.
observations.uncertainty: Annual officeholding changes do not identify candidate pipelines, party selection, committee authority, legislative outcomes, or why leadership changed in a particular country.
observations.subgroup: Women parliamentarians, Speakers, candidates, political parties, electoral administrators, legislative staff, and voters.
observations.counterinterpretation: Leadership turnover and election timing can move annual shares; formal representation may still build experience, networks, and future leadership pathways even when headline progress is slow.

denominator.unit: parliamentarians surveyed in IPU reporting on public intimidation and violence

women_public_intimidation.unit: percent of women parliamentarians surveyed who experienced violence or intimidation by the public online or offline

men_public_intimidation.unit: percent of men parliamentarians surveyed who experienced violence or intimidation by the public online or offline

participation_mechanism.value: hostility and intimidation can deter women from seeking office and slow progress toward equal political power

safety_endpoint.value: formal representation requires safe participation, not only access to seats

observations.method: IPU report synthesis using survey evidence on public intimidation and violence against parliamentarians, combined with representation data.
observations.uncertainty: The survey is not a population estimate of all politicians or citizens and does not establish that intimidation caused exit, non-candidacy, or policy change; reporting and exposure may differ by context.
observations.subgroup: Women and men parliamentarians, candidates, public officials, online communities, parties, security institutions, and journalists.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some hostility reflects public contestation that affects politicians of all genders, while stronger institutional security, platform governance, party support, and accountability may reduce unequal exposure without suppressing legitimate criticism.

observations.period: 2025 elections and parliamentary renewals; institutional rules

denominator.unit: countries that held parliamentary renewals covering 62 chambers in 2025

chambers_renewed.unit: parliamentary chambers covered by those renewals

americas_representation.unit: percent of parliamentarians who were women in the Americas as of 1 January 2026

quota_mechanism.value: well-designed and implemented quotas continued to play a critical role in increasing women's parliamentary representation

parity_cases.value: Bolivia joined Cuba, Nicaragua, Mexico, Rwanda, Andorra, and the United Arab Emirates among countries with parity or more women in the lower or single chamber

observations.method: IPU analysis of parliamentary renewals, electoral outcomes, regional representation, and quota implementation in 2025.
observations.uncertainty: Quota associations do not isolate quota design from party behavior, enforcement, electoral system, candidate supply, or broader social conditions; chamber-level parity does not prove equal influence.
observations.subgroup: Women candidates, parties, electoral-management bodies, parliaments, voters, and countries using different quota and seat-allocation rules.
observations.counterinterpretation: Quotas can widen access but may be symbolic, circumvented, or unevenly enforced; non-quota reforms, party recruitment, financing, safety, and care support may also matter.

boundary: This record adds a political-voice route linking formal representation, executive and parliamentary leadership, electoral rules, quotas, public hostility, safety, and participation. It is not a survey of general citizens, a causal estimate of women’s policy influence, proof of equal power, or a respondent-level microdata analysis.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official IPU and IPU-UN Women 2026 press-release summaries, Women in Parliament 2025 reporting, and linked official data resources were reviewed; representation, leadership, hostility, elections, quota, regional, and boundary claims were cross-checked.
